sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *aunque* from A2 Unit 28, and *a pesar de que* and *pese a* from B1 Unit 32. They let you say that something continues in spite of an obstacle, which is exactly the story of the peoples of the south and their languages. With a real fact, the verb stays in the indicative.

sections.title: Four ways to concede
rows: A pesar de las presiones, siguieron hablando zapoteco.
*a pesar de* + noun: In spite of the pressure, they kept speaking Zapotec.
A pesar de ser un trabajo lento, muchas mujeres tejen.
*a pesar de* + infinitive: Although it is slow work, many women weave.
A pesar de que la escuela enseñaba en español, hablaban su lengua en casa.
*a pesar de que* + a full clause: Although the school taught in Spanish, they spoke their language at home.
Pese a las dificultades, la tradición continúa.
*pese a* + noun: Despite the difficulties, the tradition continues.

items.spanish: A pesar de que el trabajo es lento, el telar de cintura perdura en muchos pueblos.
items.english: Although the work is slow, the backstrap loom lasts in many villages.

items.spanish: Pese a las presiones, los pueblos mixtecos conservan su lengua.
items.english: Despite the pressures, the Mixtec peoples keep their language.

items.spanish: Aunque la escuela enseñaba en español, muchas familias siguieron hablando su lengua.
items.english: Although the school taught in Spanish, many families kept speaking their language.

items.spanish: A pesar de ser muy antiguo, el huipil sigue en uso.
items.english: Although it is very old, the huipil is still in use.

sections.content: *A pesar de* and *pese a* take a noun or an infinitive; before a full clause you need *que*: *a pesar de que la escuela enseñaba en español*. Not *a pesar que*, and not *a pesar de la escuela enseñaba*. *Aunque* also takes a full clause and means nearly the same.
